note: Happy Thanksgiving. This is a daytime holiday test edition. Congress and both state legislatures are on recess, so it covers the past several days rather than just the last 24 hours, and some sections are shorter than usual.

federal.overview: The one federal labor item this holiday week is narrow but practical: Labor Department guidance on how salaried school staff qualify for family and medical leave. It matters most for school districts and other employers that do not track the hours of salaried workers.

items.headline: Labor Department: a school specialist's after-hours IEP work counts toward family-leave eligibility
items.what_changed: In an opinion letter dated Nov. 17, the Labor Department said a salaried occupational therapist's after-hours work on IEPs (individualized education programs, the legal plans for students with disabilities) must be counted as hours of service under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA). It said the therapist's travel time between schools also likely counts.
items.what_it_does: To qualify for FMLA, a worker generally needs 12 months with the employer and at least 1,250 hours of service in the past year. FMLA guarantees up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave a year. The department said that when an employer has not kept accurate hours, it is up to the employer to prove a worker does not qualify, and that for salaried workers exempt from overtime recordkeeping, eligibility is presumed after 12 months on the job.
items.who_it_affects: School districts and their salaried specialists, such as occupational therapists, speech therapists, and special education staff, and more broadly any employer that does not track salaried employees' hours. Opinion letters are guidance, not new regulations.

sources.title: School specialist's time spent on IEPs after hours may count toward FMLA eligibility

federal.overview: Medicare finished its third round of drug price negotiations, and for the first time the list includes drugs given in doctors' offices, not just pharmacy drugs. The new prices start in 2028. Separately, states are deciding whether to use the federal six-month grace period on Medicaid work requirements; Massachusetts opted in this week (see the Massachusetts health care block).

items.headline: Medicare sets negotiated prices for 13 more drugs, starting in 2028
items.status: Final negotiated prices; take effect Jan. 1, 2028
items.what_changed: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) announced negotiated prices for 13 drugs in the third round of the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program, created by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. This is the first round to include Part B drugs, which are given in a doctor's office, alongside Part D pharmacy drugs.
items.what_it_does: CMS estimates the prices would have saved Medicare $9.2 billion, about 45% of net spending, had they been in effect in 2025; counting a separate drugmaker discount program, the savings figure is about $5.5 billion (33%). Fifteen drugs were selected, but no negotiated price applies to Xeljanz and Xolair because cheaper generic or biosimilar versions are now on the market, or to Botox while a court order in a lawsuit by its maker remains in effect. In four cases the drugmaker accepted CMS's written final offer; the rest were agreed in talks.
items.who_it_affects: In 2025 about 1.4 million Part D enrollees and about 120,000 Part B enrollees used the selected drugs, which treat cancer, immune conditions, diabetes, and other chronic illnesses. CMS projects beneficiaries will save about $69 million out of pocket in Part D and $395 million in Part B once the prices apply. With this round, 37 drugs will have negotiated Medicare prices.
items.whats_next: Prices take effect Jan. 1, 2028. The Botox exclusion depends on the outcome of AbbVie v. HHS.

sources.title: CMS Announces Lower Negotiated Prices for 13 High-Cost Drugs
Fact sheet: Negotiated prices for initial price applicability year 2028

federal.overview: With federal funding set to run out Dec. 11, the Senate Appropriations Committee's plan for the Education Department differs sharply from the House's. The Senate plan would raise the department's budget 19%; the House committee's plan would cut it 10%. Congress must pass a funding bill or another stopgap by the deadline.

items.headline: Senate committee's 2027 plan would raise Education Department funding 19%; House plan would cut it 10%
items.what_changed: The Republican-led Senate Appropriations Committee proposed $93.9 billion for the Education Department in fiscal year 2027, a 19% increase over 2026.
items.what_it_does: Title I aid for schools in low-income communities ($18.4 billion), English-learner aid ($890 million), and the Office for Civil Rights ($140 million) would stay level. Special education would get $50 million more ($15.5 billion), charter schools $60 million more ($500 million), and after-school programs $5 million more ($1.3 billion). A companion health bill would add $50 million for Head Start ($12.4 billion). The House committee's plan, advanced in June, would cut the department to $71 billion, including a $2 billion cut to Title I; the president's budget asked for $76.5 billion. Subcommittee chair Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) said the plan makes meaningful investments; Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) said it does not do enough to stop the department's dismantling or invest in families.
items.who_it_affects: Public schools, especially high-poverty districts and students with disabilities, and Head Start programs. Final numbers depend on a House–Senate agreement.
items.whats_next: Current stopgap funding expires at the end of Dec. 11. Congress must pass full-year bills or another stopgap, or a shutdown begins.

sources.title: Senate committee's FY27 plan gives Education Department 19% boost

federal.label: Trade
federal.overview: The administration proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, the law it has relied on since the Supreme Court struck down tariffs imposed under an emergency-powers law in February. Nothing takes effect yet: a public comment period comes first, and officials say January is the earliest start.

items.headline: U.S. proposes new tariffs on China, the EU, and 12 other economies over 'excess capacity'
items.status: Proposed; comment period first, earliest effect about January
items.what_changed: On Nov. 25 the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) found that 14 economies' industrial policies, such as subsidies that let factories produce far more than demand supports, unreasonably burden U.S. commerce, and proposed tariffs in response. The finding follows an eight-month investigation of 16 economies; probes of Mexico and Norway continue.
items.what_it_does: China would face a new 20% tariff on top of the roughly 25% tariffs from Trump's first term, rising to 40% if a U.S.–China trade truce that expires in January breaks down; about $30 billion of Chinese imports under review for tariff cuts would be excluded. Vietnam would also face 20%. For other partners, officials said the new tariffs would replace, not add to, existing ones, and would stay within caps in earlier trade deals, such as 15% for the EU, Japan, and South Korea. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that 'when it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points.'
items.who_it_affects: U.S. importers and consumers of goods from China, the EU, India, Japan, South Korea, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, and Vietnam. Targeted sectors in the investigation included steel, cars, chips, and solar panels. China's foreign ministry called 'overcapacity' a 'false issue.'
items.whats_next: Exact rates for most countries will be published in the Federal Register, followed by a public comment period.

sources.title: Trump proposes a new wave of tariffs on China, E.U. and other trade partners
Trump admin proposes new tariffs on China, EU and 12 other trading partners
Trump unveils new tariffs on China and other U.S. trading partners

federal.label: Justice & courts
federal.overview: Two presidential directives and one court ruling this week deal with federal power: a memo telling the Justice Department to seek the death penalty more often and speed executions, an order requiring federal contractors to route congressional requests through the White House, and a judge's order stopping the FCC's early review of ABC station licenses.

items.headline: Presidential memo directs the Justice Department to seek death sentences in more cases and speed executions
items.what_changed: A memorandum to the Attorney General directs federal prosecutors, where the law allows, to take federal jurisdiction and seek the death penalty for the first-degree murder of a child and for murders committed during rape, child sexual exploitation, sex trafficking, kidnapping, or human trafficking. This adds to categories named in a January 2025 executive order.
items.what_it_does: The Attorney General must work to carry out federal death sentences 'as expeditiously as possible,' including by prioritizing quick resolution of appeals and habeas corpus petitions (court challenges to whether a prisoner is lawfully held), opposing what the memo calls 'dilatory' litigation tactics, seeking expedited court review, and cutting administrative delays. The memo does not change the law; courts still control the pace of appeals.
items.who_it_affects: Defendants in federal capital cases and people on federal death row, along with victims' families. It applies only to federal cases, not state prosecutions.

sources.title: Expeditious Enforcement of Capital Sentences and the Pursuit of Justice for Victims of Heinous Crimes

items.source_note: This is the White House's own text; no outside coverage was readable at publication time.

items.headline: Executive order requires federal contractors to notify the White House before answering Congress
items.status: Executive order signed Nov. 20; published Nov. 25
items.what_changed: An executive order requires all federal contractors and subcontractors to notify the White House and their contracting agency of any pending or future congressional request about their work or communications with the executive branch, and to follow White House instructions on withholding information the administration says is covered by executive privilege (the president's power to keep some internal communications confidential).
items.what_it_does: Agencies must inform contractors of the requirement and coordinate responses. The Office of Management and Budget will issue compliance guidance. Contractors that do not comply could face contract termination, suspension, or debarment (a ban on future federal contracts). The order says some congressional leaders have been 'harassing' contractors and that coordination avoids duplicate litigation; its legal limits have not yet been tested in court.
items.who_it_affects: Federal contractors and subcontractors of every size, and congressional committees seeking information from them, including the incoming Democratic majorities that take over in January.

sources.title: Protecting the Executive's Privileges and Enhancing Efficiencies in Federal Contracting

items.source_note: This is the White House's own text; no outside coverage was readable at publication time.

items.headline: Judge bars the FCC from an early review of eight ABC stations' licenses
items.what_changed: U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan in Washington granted Disney's request to block the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from holding a hearing on the licenses of eight ABC-owned TV stations, a step that could have led to revocation. According to Al Jazeera's report (from AP and Reuters), the judge wrote that 'this is not a close case' and that the FCC appeared to be carrying out a retaliatory campaign against ABC's free-speech rights.
items.what_it_does: FCC Chair Brendan Carr ordered the early reviews in April, although the licenses were not due for renewal until October 2028 at the earliest; the FCC had not ordered an early review in more than 50 years. The injunction keeps the review on hold while Disney's lawsuit proceeds. An FCC spokesperson called the ruling 'wrong on the facts and wrong on the law.'
items.who_it_affects: ABC stations in Los Angeles, Chicago, New York, and other cities, and other broadcasters whose licenses depend on FCC renewal.
items.whats_next: The FCC can appeal the injunction.

sources.title: US judge blocks Trump's FCC attempt to target Disney's ABC stations

federal.label: Housing
federal.overview: A new HUD rule would end federal housing aid for 'mixed-status' families, households where at least one member lacks eligible immigration status. Twenty-one states, including Massachusetts, have sued to stop it before it takes effect Dec. 14.

items.headline: 21 states, including Massachusetts, sue to block HUD rule ending housing aid for mixed-status families
items.status: Final rule takes effect Dec. 14; lawsuit filed
items.what_changed: The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) finalized a rule that would deny federal housing assistance to a household if any member lacks eligible citizenship or immigration status. Twenty-one states and Pennsylvania's governor sued to block it.
items.what_it_does: For more than 30 years, mixed-status families have received prorated aid, reduced to exclude the ineligible member. The rule would end aid for the whole household, require everyone to verify status, and require housing authorities and private landlords to report tenants who fail verification to the Department of Homeland Security. HUD Secretary Scott Turner said the rule enforces a 1980 law and frees up to $218 million for eligible Americans on waitlists; the states argue Congress never gave HUD this power and that U.S.-citizen children could lose their homes.
items.who_it_affects: HUD and DHS identified about 20,000 mixed-status households receiving federal housing aid nationwide. California's attorney general estimated 7,000 households in that state alone.
items.whats_next: The rule takes effect Dec. 14 unless a court blocks it.

sources.title: Mass. joins 20 states in suing HUD over a rule that could cut off housing aid for mixed-status families

massachusetts.overview: A months-long labor dispute at one of Boston's biggest hospitals is over. More than 4,000 Brigham and Women's nurses ratified a contract that limits the hospital's use of temporary travel nurses.

items.headline: Brigham and Women's nurses ratify contract, ending threat of an open-ended strike
items.status: Contract ratified Nov. 24; runs through Sept. 30, 2028
items.what_changed: Nurses at Brigham and Women's Hospital voted to ratify a contract with Mass General Brigham, ending a dispute that included a five-day work stoppage in July and a planned open-ended strike called off when a tentative deal was reached Nov. 11.
items.what_it_does: The contract limits the use of temporary travel nurses, keeps current nurses' health insurance affordable, adds two pay steps for nurses at the top of the scale, and gives all nurses a prorated $1,000 bonus, according to the Massachusetts Nurses Association.
items.who_it_affects: More than 4,000 Brigham nurses and the hospital's patients. The union did not release the vote count.

sources.title: Brigham nurses ratify contract, ending monthslong labor fight

massachusetts.overview: Massachusetts is using every available delay on new federal Medicaid work rules, while a state bill to strengthen primary care remains stuck in House–Senate talks. Both stories turn on deadlines: Jan. 1 for the federal rules and Jan. 5 for the Legislature's session.

items.headline: MassHealth opts into six-month grace period on federal Medicaid work rules
items.status: State decision announced Nov. 24; grace period Jan. 1–June 30, 2027
items.what_changed: MassHealth, the state's Medicaid program, said it will use the optional six-month 'hold harmless' period offered by the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Members who would otherwise lose eligibility on Jan. 1, 2027, under the new federal work and education requirements will not be cut off before June 30, 2027.
items.what_it_does: During the grace period the state will check whether members meet or are exempt from the requirements, created by the 2025 federal budget law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, but will not deny or end coverage solely for not meeting them. MassHealth also joined a multi-state request for a 'good faith effort' exemption that would delay the requirements altogether until July 1, 2027. It urged members to start meeting the requirements anyway.
items.who_it_affects: About 310,000 MassHealth members are projected to be subject to the new requirements. The Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts Foundation has projected the eligibility changes could double the state's uninsured rate.
items.whats_next: Enforcement would begin July 1, 2027, unless the federal exemption request is granted or Congress changes the law.

sources.title: MassHealth opts into 6-month grace period on Medicaid work rules

items.headline: Primary care bill still in House–Senate talks with about six weeks left in the session
items.status: In conference committee since July 31; session ends Jan. 5
items.what_changed: Negotiators have not agreed on a final bill to expand primary care access and lower prescription drug costs. The House passed its version 158–0 and the Senate 35–4.
items.what_it_does: Both versions would require hospitals and health systems to devote 15% of their spending to primary care without raising overall costs. The Senate sets a 2030 deadline; the House would allow until 2036. The Senate would require one uniform primary care payment model for all systems; the House would let each system design its own. The Senate's lead negotiator, Sen. Cindy Friedman, said 'we must get something done now'; the House's, Rep. Aaron Michlewitz, said lawmakers are 'trying to find the right balance.'
items.who_it_affects: Patients who wait months for a primary care appointment, primary care doctors, and hospital systems whose budgets would shift.
items.whats_next: Any bill not passed by Jan. 5 must start over in the new session.

sources.title: Mass. lawmakers' talks over primary care bill face deadline

massachusetts.label: Energy
massachusetts.overview: The governor's energy affordability bill, meant to cut ratepayer costs by about $10 billion over a decade, is one of 13 bills still in House–Senate talks. The Senate's energy chair now puts its chances at 50-50.

items.headline: Energy affordability bill's chances '50-50,' Senate negotiator says
items.status: In conference committee; session ends Jan. 5
items.what_changed: Sen. Michael Barrett, the Senate's lead negotiator, said talks 'have not gone particularly well' and gave the bill a '50-50 chance' this session. His House counterpart, Rep. Mark Cusack, said he is optimistic a deal can be reached.
items.what_it_does: All versions aim to save ratepayers about $10 billion over 10 years, partly by expanding state energy purchasing and tightening rules for competitive electric suppliers, third-party companies that often charge more than utilities. The House version cuts $1 billion from Mass Save, the efficiency program funded by a charge on utility bills, and would lift the ban on new nuclear plants; the Senate version keeps Mass Save's budget, keeps the nuclear ban, and would end a costly gas-pipeline replacement program by 2030. Eversource wrote that neither bill would improve affordability; Barrett called that letter an attempt to sink the bill, while Cusack said stakeholder input is routine.
items.who_it_affects: Massachusetts electricity and gas customers, whose bills are among the highest in the nation; utilities; and the state's climate targets.
items.whats_next: Deadline to pass legislation this session is Jan. 5, 2027.

sources.title: 'We're at a sensitive moment': As legislative deadline nears, energy affordability negotiations enter scramble mode

massachusetts.label: Immigration & courts
massachusetts.overview: Massachusetts is in federal court over whether its new courthouse law can bind federal immigration agents. The state says ICE is violating the law; the federal government says states cannot direct federal law enforcement.

items.headline: Massachusetts sues ICE over arrests in state courthouses
items.what_changed: Attorney General Andrea Campbell sued to stop U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) from arresting people in and around state courthouses. The suit says at least 38 such arrests have occurred since the courthouse provision of the state's PROTECT Act took effect Nov. 3.
items.what_it_does: The PROTECT Act requires officers to show court officials a judicial warrant (signed by a judge) before making a civil arrest, such as for an immigration violation, at a courthouse. The state argues the Tenth Amendment gives it authority over its own courts and that the arrests derail criminal cases. A Homeland Security spokesperson called courthouse arrests 'common sense' because officers know where a person will be and that the person has passed security screening.
items.who_it_affects: Immigrants with state court dates, including defendants, victims, and witnesses, and the state's criminal courts.

sources.title: Mass. sues ICE over immigration arrests in state courts

massachusetts.label: Transportation
massachusetts.overview: One bill did finish this fall: an expansion of the 'Move Over' law, which Gov. Healey says she will sign.

items.headline: Expanded 'Move Over' law heads to Healey, who says she will sign it
items.status: Passed Legislature; governor says she will sign
items.what_changed: The Legislature sent the governor a compromise bill expanding the state's 'Move Over' law, which requires drivers to change lanes or slow down when passing emergency vehicles stopped with flashing lights. Healey said, 'It's a matter of public safety… I'm glad that it's on my desk.'
items.what_it_does: The bill adds utility vehicles and disabled vehicles to the list of protected vehicles and raises penalties. Earlier versions required repeat offenders to complete a driver program run by the Registry of Motor Vehicles. WBUR described the bill as bringing 'larger fines and more cars' under the law; the final fine amounts were not available in a readable source at publication time.
items.who_it_affects: All Massachusetts drivers, plus utility crews, tow operators, and stranded motorists on the roadside.
items.whats_next: Takes effect after the governor signs it, on the schedule set in the bill.

sources.title: WBUR Today: Healey plans to sign Move Over bill
Larger fines and more cars: What to know about the Mass. bill to expand the state's 'Move Over' law

new_hampshire.overview: A year after a New Hampshire Bulletin investigation found hundreds of cases of abuse and neglect in the state's disability care system, the state health department has answered a review committee's recommendations. It agreed to work on some but warned that money may limit what it can do.

items.headline: State health department responds to disability-system reforms, citing budget limits
items.what_changed: The Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) responded to recommendations from the System Review Committee of the state's Developmental Services Quality Council. It agreed to work with stakeholders on some points, but Commissioner Lori Weaver wrote that its ability to act on several recommendations 'will ultimately be determined by the current fiscal environment.'
items.what_it_does: The committee's top requests include one centralized intake and triage system with the abuse hotline built in, replacing several separate agencies and procedures; a clear leadership structure for investigations; and more public reporting and analysis of data. Committee members called the response insufficient; co-chair Stephanie Patrick said DHHS focuses on 'compliance' rather than the quality of care. Gov. Kelly Ayotte's office said DHHS's response speaks for the state.
items.who_it_affects: People with developmental disabilities such as autism or cerebral palsy who receive taxpayer-funded care, their families, and provider agencies.
items.whats_next: Funding for changes would come through the next two-year state budget, which the new Legislature will write in 2027.

sources.title: State responds to committee recommendations on addressing issues in NH's disability system (New Hampshire Bulletin, republished)

items.source_note: Reported by the New Hampshire Bulletin; read via its republished copy on Yahoo News because the Bulletin's site blocked automated reading.

new_hampshire.overview: A new report says fewer New Hampshire graduates go to college, and more of those who do leave the state, even as the fastest-growing jobs require degrees. New Hampshire ranks last in public funding for higher education.

items.headline: Report: fewer NH graduates go to college, and most four-year students leave the state
items.status: New report (New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute, Nov. 24)
items.what_changed: An analysis from the New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute found that between 2014 and 2024, the number of high school graduates fell about 5%, but the number going on to college fell nearly three times as fast. Three in five graduates who pursue a four-year degree leave the state.
items.what_it_does: The report recommends making public colleges more affordable and expanding enrollment options. It notes the state ranks last in public higher education funding, that the last budget cut University System of New Hampshire support by about $18 million over two years, and that the system raised tuition this year for the first time in several years. Six of the state's 10 fastest-growing occupations require a four-year degree. The University of New Hampshire raised enrollment nearly 5% this year, which it partly credits to a record $40 million in financial aid.
items.who_it_affects: New Hampshire high school students and families, the state's public colleges, and employers needing degree holders.

sources.title: Report says fewer NH students are pursuing the college degrees that employers want

new_hampshire.label: Local aid & property taxes
new_hampshire.overview: With the new Legislature sworn in next week, some mayors are filing bills to shift costs from local property taxes back to the state, especially for pensions, education, and shared tax revenue.

items.headline: Mayors file bills to restore state aid to cities and towns
items.what_changed: Laconia Mayor Mike Bordes, also a newly elected state representative, has filed bills to raise the share of state meals and rooms tax revenue returned to municipalities from 30% to 40% over four years, and to have the state again pay part of local pension costs.
items.what_it_does: The state once paid 40% of local contributions to the New Hampshire Retirement System for police, firefighters, and teachers, then cut that share over time to nothing; Bordes's bill would restore it to 17.5%. Somersworth Mayor Matt Gerding said towns need more state education funding and described 'a decade of cuts' pushed down to local property taxpayers.
items.who_it_affects: Property taxpayers and municipal budgets statewide, and local police, fire, and school employees whose pensions cities must fund.
items.whats_next: The new Legislature is sworn in next week; bills get hearings in the new year.

sources.title: New Hampshire mayors hope for local aid changes under new Legislature

new_hampshire.label: Courts
new_hampshire.overview: A second justice is leaving the New Hampshire Supreme Court this year, which will leave the five-seat court with three sitting justices until the governor fills the seats.

items.headline: Justice Bryan Gould to retire, leaving two vacancies on the NH Supreme Court
items.status: Retirement announced Nov. 23; leaving before year's end
items.what_changed: Associate Justice Bryan Gould announced he will step down for health and family reasons before the end of the year. He is the second justice to leave in two months, after Chief Justice Gordon MacDonald resigned in September following a judicial conduct investigation.
items.what_it_does: With no nominee yet for MacDonald's seat, the five-member court will have three sitting justices. In New Hampshire the governor nominates justices and the Executive Council confirms them. The court said Gould will spend his remaining weeks finishing opinions in cases he has heard.
items.who_it_affects: Anyone with a case before the state's highest court, where cases may be decided by a smaller panel until the seats are filled.

sources.title: NH Supreme Court Justice Bryan Gould retires due to health concerns

ai.label: Government & regulation
ai.overview: States keep moving on AI while Congress prepares to take up a national framework in January. New York enacted a five-year ban on AI chatbot toys for young children, and the nation's governors released bipartisan principles asking Congress to keep a role for states.

items.headline: New York enacts five-year ban on AI chatbot toys for children 12 and under
items.status: Signed into law Nov. 24 (Chapter 416); takes effect in February
items.what_changed: Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a bill (S.9408A) banning the sale of children's toys with a built-in 'AI companion' for five years. New York is the second state to ban such toys, after California, NBC News reported.
items.what_it_does: The law defines an AI companion as a system designed to simulate an ongoing human-like relationship, for example by remembering past conversations, asking unprompted emotional questions, or keeping up personal dialogue. 'Children's toy' follows the federal definition: a product meant for children 12 or younger. The law also orders an interagency study by the Department of State, the Office of Mental Health, the Attorney General, and others. Hochul signed it with an approval memo, which in New York usually means agreed changes will follow.
items.who_it_affects: Toy makers and retailers selling in New York, and families with young children.
items.whats_next: Takes effect in February; the ban expires after five years unless extended.

sources.title: New York governor Kathy Hochul signs AI toy ban into law
Senate Bill S9408A: bill text, summary, and actions

items.headline: Governors release bipartisan principles for state and federal AI rules
items.what_changed: The National Governors Association released principles for AI governance developed by a bipartisan council led by Govs. Wes Moore (D-Md.), Mike Braun (R-Ind.), Josh Stein (D-N.C.), and Spencer Cox (R-Utah). They are meant to make state laws more consistent and to inform the incoming Congress as it writes a federal AI framework.
items.what_it_does: The principles say both levels of government should regulate: Washington should focus on national and international risks, while states keep the power to govern AI use within their own responsibilities. They call for policies that promote innovation, protect the public, especially children and consumers, and give workers a voice in how AI is deployed. Moore said governors 'agree that humans must stay in control.'
items.who_it_affects: State governments and legislatures, AI companies operating across many states, and workers and consumers covered by state AI laws. The principles are not binding.
items.whats_next: The new Congress takes office in January.

sources.title: Governors Call for AI Action

ai.label: AI in schools
ai.overview: Google's decision not to offer schools a version of its search engine without AI features is drawing pushback from parents, educators, and some of its own employees. Districts with money are building workarounds; smaller ones may not be able to.

items.headline: Google won't offer schools search without AI features; employees and parents push back
items.what_changed: Google said it will not separate AI features from its education tools. More than 550 Google employees signed a petition asking the company to let schools use Search without AI Overviews, and parents and educators protested outside Google offices in six cities, NPR reported.
items.what_it_does: Schools that turn off Google's AI features for students would lose Google Search as well. Google did not comment to NPR. Some districts are building their own filters: Fairfax County, Va., is piloting a tool that blocks AI on school devices. Experts NPR spoke with said smaller, less-funded districts may not be able to do the same.
items.who_it_affects: Students and teachers in the many districts that use Google's education software, and district technology staff.

sources.title: Google employees protest AI in schools policy

ai.label: Industry
ai.overview: Federal regulators have cleared a plan to put AI computing in orbit. Demand for AI computing keeps rising, and communities have pushed back on large data centers built on the ground.

items.headline: FCC approves SpaceX plan for up to 1 million 'space data center' satellites
items.what_changed: According to the Washington Examiner, the Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX's plan to put as many as 1 million satellites into orbit that can work as data centers, the computing facilities that power AI.
items.what_it_does: SpaceX applied in January for authority to run what it calls an 'Orbital Data Center' system; the FCC accepted the filing for public comment in February. The Washington Examiner describes the approval as a major step for orbital data centers, which companies are exploring as an alternative to large ground-based data centers that strain local power and water supplies.
items.who_it_affects: AI developers that need computing capacity, communities facing data center construction, and other satellite operators and astronomers concerned about crowded orbits.

sources.title: FCC approves SpaceX's plan to launch 1 million 'space data center' satellites

items.source_note: Only the opening of the Washington Examiner article was readable, and no second outlet or FCC document confirming the approval was found at publication time.

world.label: Middle East
world.overview: The U.S.–Israeli war with Iran, which began in late February, is again spreading to Gulf states that host U.S. forces. Negotiations are deadlocked, and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz are at their highest level of the war.

items.headline: Two Italian technicians killed in drone attack on a facility in Kuwait
items.what_changed: Italy's foreign ministry said two Italian technicians working for the German arms maker Rheinmetall died after an Iranian strike on a facility in Kuwait. Kuwait's defense ministry said Iranian drones were intercepted and four people, the two Italians plus a Kuwaiti and a Pakistani, were hit by falling shrapnel.
items.what_it_does: An Iranian armed forces spokesperson denied that Iran's military carried out any operation. The attack came just over a week after Kuwait said it repelled Iranian drones aimed at an airbase hosting U.S. forces, the first strikes on Kuwait in more than two months.
items.who_it_affects: Foreign workers and residents in Gulf states hosting U.S. forces, and countries with citizens in the region. Recent exchanges have raised fears of a wider escalation.

sources.title: Italy says two citizens killed in Iranian strike in Kuwait

world.label: Asia
world.overview: North Korea's leader called for broader deployment of tactical nuclear weapons, short-range weapons meant for battlefield use, amid a border dispute with South Korea. Myanmar's leader said the country will not comply with parts of last week's World Court genocide ruling (see International law).

items.headline: Kim Jong Un calls for deploying tactical nuclear weapons 'across multiple domains'
items.what_changed: During an inspection of nuclear material and weapons facilities, Kim Jong Un said North Korea is systematically expanding its nuclear material production and urged deploying tactical nuclear weapons 'for different missions,' according to state media KCNA as reported by Al Jazeera and Reuters.
items.what_it_does: Kim said any attempt to deny North Korea's status as a nuclear-weapons state, which it wrote into its constitution in 2023, would be treated as 'an open declaration of war.' The statement comes amid a dispute over a September landmine blast in the demilitarized zone that injured three South Korean soldiers; a joint South Korea–UN investigation blamed the North, which then fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles.
items.who_it_affects: South Korea, Japan, and U.S. forces in the region. South Korea estimates the North has 80 to 120 nuclear warheads.

sources.title: Kim Jong Un says North Korea should widen deployment of tactical nukes

world.label: International law
world.overview: Myanmar, the first state ever found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention, says it will not comply with parts of the ruling. The UN's top court has no police force; enforcement depends largely on the Security Council and other states.

items.headline: Myanmar says it will not comply with 'inappropriate' parts of World Court genocide ruling
items.status: Government response to International Court of Justice ruling
items.what_changed: Min Aung Hlaing, the coup leader who is now Myanmar's president, said the country 'would not comply with requirements it considered inappropriate' in last week's International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruling, according to state media. He did not say which parts.
items.what_it_does: As the BBC reports, the ICJ ruled 9–6 that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority in 2017 military operations in Rakhine State. The court found about 10,000 Rohingya were killed and about 815,000 were targeted, and more than 700,000 fled to Bangladesh. The case was brought by The Gambia in 2019. Myanmar denies genocide and says its forces responded to attacks by armed groups.
items.who_it_affects: Rohingya refugees, most of them in camps in Bangladesh, and Rohingya still in Myanmar; also the credibility of the Genocide Convention.

sources.title: Myanmar refuses to comply with parts of ICJ genocide ruling

world.label: Africa & global health
world.overview: Africa has a major advance in HIV prevention and a worsening Ebola crisis at the same time. A cheap generic version of a twice-yearly HIV prevention shot has begun arriving. Meanwhile, Congo's Ebola outbreak has passed 12,000 cases as fighting disrupts the response, and a Kenyan court halted a U.S.-backed quarantine site.

items.headline: Low-cost generic HIV prevention shot begins arriving in Africa
items.what_changed: The first global shipment of generic lenacapavir, an injection given twice a year that prevents HIV infection, arrived in Zambia, the Global Fund said. Uganda is next, and Zimbabwe follows early next year.
items.what_it_does: The generic is expected to cost about $40 per person per year, compared with about $28,000 a year for the original Gilead version in the U.S. In a 2024 trial of more than 5,000 young women and girls in Uganda and South Africa, none who received the shot contracted HIV. The World Health Organization recommended it for prevention in July 2025. Health experts say a twice-yearly shot avoids the daily pills and stigma of current prevention drugs.
items.who_it_affects: People at risk of HIV across sub-Saharan Africa, where the disease burden is highest, and national health programs that buy prevention drugs.

sources.title: Hope for millions as cheaper HIV prevention jab reaches Africa

items.headline: Congo's Ebola outbreak passes 12,000 cases as fighting forces out health workers
items.what_changed: The Democratic Republic of the Congo has confirmed at least 12,021 Ebola infections and 5,904 deaths, according to government data reported by Al Jazeera, AP, and Reuters. Response workers have had to leave affected areas as fighting intensifies in Ituri province.
items.what_it_does: The outbreak, declared in mid-May, is caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola, for which there is no approved treatment or vaccine. Cases are now in eight of the country's 26 provinces. A WHO official said about a dozen people, including two WHO staff, were evacuated after three days trapped in a hospital amid crossfire between the army and an armed group.
items.who_it_affects: Residents of eastern Congo and neighboring countries, and health and aid workers in conflict areas.

sources.title: DR Congo Ebola cases surpass 12,000 as fighting disrupts response in east

items.headline: Kenyan court halts U.S.-backed Ebola quarantine site, citing lack of public disclosure
items.what_changed: Kenya's High Court ruled that the government violated the constitution by allowing construction of a U.S.-backed Ebola quarantine facility at Laikipia airbase near Nanyuki without disclosing the agreement or seeking public input, Al Jazeera reported, citing Reuters.
items.what_it_does: The court ordered all further work stopped until the government discloses the U.S. agreement and holds public participation. The 50-bed facility was built to quarantine people exposed to Ebola, including U.S. citizens; seven American aid workers stayed there in July. Protests against the site have turned deadly.
items.who_it_affects: Residents of Laikipia County, and U.S. and international aid workers responding to Congo's outbreak who would be quarantined there.

sources.title: Kenya gov't violated constitution with Ebola quarantine site, court says

world.label: Europe
world.overview: Ukraine's U.S.-built fighter jets are wearing out. A pending U.S. sale of spare parts is aimed at returning grounded F-16s to service while peace talks remain stalled.

items.headline: State Department approves possible $622 million sale of F-16 parts to Ukraine
items.status: Proposed foreign military sale approved by State Department
items.what_changed: According to the Washington Examiner, the State Department approved the possible sale of $621.9 million in critical F-16 fighter jet parts to Ukraine.
items.what_it_does: The Washington Examiner reports that much of Ukraine's F-16 fleet, all older models supplied by the U.S. and allies, is grounded by maintenance problems from heavy use, and that the parts could return aircraft to service. Ukraine has relied on the F-16s for air defense against Russian missiles and drones.
items.who_it_affects: Ukraine's air force and air defenses. Congress has a review period before arms sales go ahead.

sources.title: State Department approves possible sale to Ukraine of critical F-16 parts

items.source_note: Only the opening of the Washington Examiner article was readable, and no official notice was found at publication time.
